Transportation

Protect the structure by fixing the channel beneath it.

Bridges, culverts, embankments and approaches sit where water concentrates. Scour and bank retreat work out of sight until they threaten the structure, the roadbed or the track.

What we see in transportation.

What you're seeingWhat's driving itHow we solve it
What you're seeing

Scour at bridge piers or abutments.

Bed material is disappearing around foundations and the channel is deepening at the crossing.

What's driving it

The crossing constricts the channel, accelerating flow that strips material from around the structure.

How we solve it

We investigate the scour at the crossing and design articulating concrete protection that conforms to the bed around piers and abutments.

What you're seeing

The bank is retreating under a rail subgrade or highway approach.

The embankment is steepening, slumping or losing ground to the channel beside it.

What's driving it

Channel migration pushing high-velocity flow into the bank that carries the subgrade or approach.

How we solve it

We redirect the flow away from the embankment and armor the bank so the subgrade keeps its support.

What you're seeing

A culvert outlet is eroding.

A scour hole has formed at the outlet, the apron is undercut, or the embankment above it is slumping.

What's driving it

Concentrated, high-velocity discharge leaving the culvert with nothing to dissipate it.

How we solve it

We engineer outlet protection sized to the discharge and install it without taking the crossing out of service.

What you're seeing

Roadside channels are cutting down.

Ditches and drainage channels are deepening, side slopes are eroding and headcuts are forming.

What's driving it

Runoff from paved surfaces on steep grades, carried at velocities the channel lining cannot resist.

How we solve it

We line the channel with a connected system that follows the grade, with vegetation where the flow allows it.

In the field

Debris and high flows scoured this creek crossing until the line beneath it was exposed. We restored the cover and rebuilt the crossing over new culverts.

Runoff cut this drainage channel deep into red clay and exposed the line running through it. We rebuilt it as a lined channel that holds its grade.

A headcut was cutting its way upstream through open ground, taking more land with every storm. Stepped grade control stopped it where it stood.

Meandering creeks see changing water levels and flow rates, and they can expose a pipeline quickly. We rebuilt this bank as a stepped wall over the line.

Over time, erosion can leave a line spanning a gap it was never meant to cross. That calls for prompt work: support beneath the line and armoring around it.

The river was taking this bank, and the farmland above it, a little more with every high water. Five years after the work, the bank is rebuilt and green.

Runoff at this processing plant had carved the drainage under the pipe racks into open ditches. We lined the channel to protect the ground the supports stand on.

When a river starts cutting toward a transmission line, the structures beside it are next. We protect the banks and channels that utility lines depend on.
